rationale: This retries round 1's per-study harmonization without the crash. The four studies differ in sequencing depth, 16S region and protocol, so a pooled forest can split on study-specific abundance levels instead of disease signal. This version z-scores log10 genus relative abundances within each study. It builds the result in a fresh writable numpy array, because round 1 crashed writing into a read-only DataFrame view. Each sample is then described relative to its own study, which should help within-study AUROC.

Lower gut microbial diversity is one of the most consistent signs of IBD, but a random forest on genus abundances only sees it indirectly. This change adds four alpha-diversity features to the genus relative abundances: Shannon entropy, inverse Simpson, observed richness, and expected rarefied richness at 1000 reads. The rarefied richness uses the hypergeometric formula, so it is deterministic and comparable across studies with very different sequencing depths.

IBD signals show up at several taxonomic ranks, such as Enterobacteriaceae gaining, Ruminococcaceae/Lachnospiraceae declining, and Proteobacteria/Firmicutes shifts. The baseline only uses genera keyed by bare genus name, so every unassigned `g__` OTU is lumped into one meaningless column, and family- or phylum-wide shifts are spread thinly across many genera. This change aggregates relative abundance at every rank from phylum to genus using full-lineage keys and feeds them all to the same random forest. That gives the forest coarser, cross-study-comparable features and keeps unclassified genera separated by family.

Lineage-merged genera from four studies with different 16S regions and depths include many rare or study-specific genera. These mostly add noise, or let the forest pick up study artifacts, and with `max_features='sqrt'` they also dilute the chance that informative genera are tried at each split. This change keeps only genera detected in at least 10% of training samples, a label-free prevalence filter computed inside each training fold, so the forest focuses on consistently measured taxa.

Case/control ratios differ a lot between studies. A pooled forest can therefore gain impurity by splitting on study-specific taxa that only encode "this study is mostly cases", which does nothing for within-study AUROC. This change keeps the features as they are and reweights the training samples so every (study, class) cell carries equal total weight. Study then no longer predicts the label, so splits should favour disease signal shared across studies.

I'm averaging the ranks of the current forest's predictions with those of an L2 logistic regression. The regression uses CLR-transformed genus abundances (log pseudocount, prevalence-filtered) and the same (study, class)-balanced weights. IBD dysbiosis shows up as smooth log-fold shifts across many taxa, such as loss of Faecalibacterium/Roseburia and gain of Enterobacteriaceae. A linear log-ratio model captures that consistently across studies, and complements the forest's threshold splits on raw proportions, which depend on sequencing depth.

The CLR branch currently adds a fixed pseudocount of 1e-5 to proportions. This makes "zero" mean different things across studies with very different sequencing depth: at 5k reads a zero means "<2e-4", at 50k reads it means "<2e-5". So shallow-sequenced samples get artificially extreme negative log-ratios that track study depth rather than disease. I replace it with a depth-aware count-scale pseudocount, log((proportion·depth + 0.5)/depth), which is a Bayesian-style zero replacement at half a read. This needs per-sample depth carried from `featurize` as an extra label-free column. The random forest branch is unchanged.

I'm making one change, to the logistic regression branch only: its CLR genus features are now z-scored within each study, while the random forest branch stays the same. Region, depth and protocol differences shift log-ratios by study. Balanced weights alone don't stop the linear model from fitting those offsets, so this should make it learn only the within-study case/control contrast that the metric scores. Test samples are standardized with their own study's statistics, which use no labels.

The metric is within-study AUROC, but the two models are rank-averaged across all test samples pooled together. The RF works on raw proportions, so its scores cluster by study. Inside one study, its pooled ranks then cover only a narrow band, and the LR effectively dominates in some studies and is drowned out in others. This change converts each model's scores to ranks within each test study before averaging, so both models get equal weight inside every study (a label-free, per-study normalization of the outputs).

I'm adding family-level CLR features, keyed by full lineage, to the logistic-regression branch alongside the genus CLR features. The random forest branch is unchanged. The main IBD shifts (Enterobacteriaceae gain, Ruminococcaceae/Lachnospiraceae loss) act across whole families. Genus calls differ between studies because each used a different 16S region and classifier depth, and every unclassified `g__` OTU is lumped into one column. Family log-ratios, z-scored within each study, should give the linear model a signal that is steadier and transfers better across studies. Round 4 failed only because it gave all ranks to the forest, which this change does not do.

The logistic-regression branch uses a fixed L2 strength, C=0.05, picked by hand. How strongly to shrink log-ratio effects depends on how consistent the IBD signal is across these four heterogeneous studies, and no single default reflects that. This change picks C by an inner grouped 5-fold CV on each training fold, grouped by subject and scored by mean within-study AUROC, which mirrors the outer metric. The random forest branch and the features stay the same.

I'm adding three OTU-level alpha-diversity features to the logistic-regression branch only: Shannon entropy, log inverse Simpson, and log expected rarefied richness at 1000 reads (hypergeometric). Like the CLR genera, they are z-scored within each study, and the random forest keeps the same genus proportions. Lower diversity is one of the most consistent IBD signals across cohorts. Round 3 put raw diversity into the forest, where depth and region offsets between studies swamped it. Within-study standardization in a linear model should keep only each sample's diversity relative to its own study, which is what within-study AUROC scores.

I'm adding a third branch to the rank average: a shallow, regularized LightGBM on the same within-study z-scored CLR genera, with the same (study, class)-balanced weights. The forest sees raw proportions, which carry depth offsets, and the logistic regression is purely additive. Boosted trees on harmonized log-ratios can pick up non-linear threshold effects and interactions, such as an Enterobacteriaceae bloom only when butyrate producers are depleted, so they should add a complementary ranking.

The (study, class)-balanced weights give samples from small studies very large weights. A fully grown forest can then spend leaves isolating single heavy samples, which fits study-specific noise and gives jagged, overconfident scores. Setting `min_samples_leaf=5` in the random forest makes each leaf average over several samples. That should give smoother rankings that rely on signal shared across studies, which is what within-study AUROC rewards. The logistic-regression branch and the features are unchanged.

Some cohorts (Engstrand, Huttenhower and Alm are longitudinal) have several stool samples per subject. Right now each sample gets equal weight inside its (study, class) cell, so subjects with many repeat samples dominate both models and their individual microbiome quirks get learned as "disease signal". This change weights each sample by 1/(that subject's number of samples) before balancing the (study, class) cells, so every subject counts once. Subject ids come from `ctx["groups_train"]` and no labels are involved. If every subject has one sample, the result is identical to the current solution.

I'm adding one feature to the logistic-regression branch only: Gevers' microbial dysbiosis index. It is computed per sample as the log of total IBD-enriched families (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae, Neisseriaceae, Veillonellaceae, Gemellaceae) over total IBD-depleted taxa (Bacteroidales, Clostridiales excluding Veillonellaceae, Erysipelotrichaceae, Bifidobacteriaceae), then z-scored within each study. It was derived in the RISK cohort and replicated elsewhere, and it pools many weak, sparse per-genus shifts into one low-noise log-ratio. Under L2 shrinkage the linear model can use that single direction cheaply and consistently across studies.

I'm changing how the logistic-regression branch harmonizes features. Instead of z-scoring CLR genera and the dysbiosis index within each study, each feature is now rank-transformed within its study and mapped to normal scores (a rank-based inverse normal transform). CLR values are zero-inflated and heavy-tailed, and how much they spread depends on each study's depth and region, so mean/SD scaling still lets outliers and study-specific tails drive the linear model. The rank transform is label-free and keeps only each sample's position within its own study, which is what within-study AUROC scores.

The random forest is now the only branch that still sees un-harmonized features. Its threshold splits on raw genus proportions mix studies, so "Enterobacteriaceae > 1%" means something different in each study because 16S region, depth and protocol differ. This change gives the forest each genus proportion rank-transformed within its own study (the same label-free inverse-normal transform that improved the LR branch in round 18). That transform is monotone inside each study, so within-study orderings stay the same and only the cross-study offsets that the forest could split on are removed. Round 2 tried a similar idea, but with no sample balancing and with fully grown trees.

This adds the HMP2 (Lloyd-Price 2019) dysbiosis score as one more feature in the logistic-regression branch. For each sample, it is the median Bray–Curtis distance on genus proportions to the training controls of the same study. Same-subject controls are excluded, so repeat samples don't shrink the distance. The score is then rank-normalized within study like the other features. IBD shows up as a sample sitting far from its own cohort's healthy reference. The score captures that as a whole-community deviation, measured against controls from the same protocol, so region and depth effects largely cancel. Neither the per-genus CLR features nor the fixed-family MDI encode this.
